newsitem.title: INDIA: Japan cautions India, Pakistan over nuclear treaty.
newsitem.headline: Japan cautions India, Pakistan over nuclear treaty.

text.p: Japan warned India and Pakistan on Friday that political and economic ties with the South Asian rivals could deteriorate unless they signed a global pact banning nuclear test explosions.

"The affinity of the Japanese people with India and Pakistan is hampered to a large degree by the fact that India and Pakistan, inflicted with tension over the Kashmir issue, and competing in missile development and deployment, have yet to sign the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT)," Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told a business seminar in New Delhi.

"When India and Pakistan as leading nations in South Asia are in contention with each other, the overall relations between Japan and South Asia, including political and economic ones, might be headed towards contraction rather than expansion."
Japan is both countries' biggest donor and is India's largest trade partner after the United States and the European Union.
Neither India nor Pakistan, which have fought three wars over the past 50 years, has endorsed the CTBT negotiated in Geneva last year.
The two neighbours say they have no nuclear weapons but experts say either can swiftly assemble them.
After three years of tense silence, New Delhi and Islamabad began fresh peace talks in March.
Ikeda, who arrived in India on Wednesday after a tour of Pakistan, said Japan was more sensitive to matters of nuclear arms control than any other nation.
"The two countries should heed the voice of the international society which deems the CTBT an important step towards nuclear disarmament," the foreign minister said.
Japan is the only country in the world to have been devastated by a nuclear attack.

But despite Japan's hard line towards the CTBT in public, Indian diplomats said Ikeda had mentioned it only in passing in discussions with Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and junior Foreign Minister Kamla Sinha.

"This statement is mainly for domestic consumption. They know our position on the CTBT and we know theirs, and we both know better than to try to change them," a senior Indian diplomat told Reuters after Ikeda's speech.
"Japan, of course, is covered by the U.S. nuclear umbrella," another Indian diplomat said.

Ikeda earlier said: "I fully understand that national security is essential to any nation's existence. I am also aware of the fact that defence policy often allows little room for compromise, and I also understand the background and logic behind India and Pakistan's unique national security policies."

India has refused to back the CTBT, saying it permits the five nuclear powers -- Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States -- to refine their nuclear arsenals and does not commit them to disarm.

The first country to suggest a nuclear test ban pact in 1954, India says the CTBT in its present form is flawed as it outlaws only test blasts, and not sophisticated forms of testing such as sub-critical nuclear tests that the United States conducted this month.
Pakistan says it will not sign the pact unless India does first. On his visit to Pakistan, Ikeda urged Islamabad to endorse the treaty first.
